section: What we assume you already know
text:
What we assume you already know
You’ve used R, Stata, or another statistical package to open a dataset and join two tables. This is not an R lesson. It’s about what goes wrong when you link individual-level data to neighborhood-level data, and how to catch it, in whichever language you use.

title: Before You Join
text:
What’s out of scope
Geocoding street addresses to census tracts. The synthetic dataset includes addresses, and we’ll point at how you’d do it, but it isn’t part of this session.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
What NaNDA is published at
NaNDA describes neighborhoods, not people. Every measure is a count, a density, or a rate for a geographic unit in a given year. There are no individual records anywhere in the archive, which is why the linking is on you: NaNDA cannot know where your participants live.
Today we use two datasets:

NaNDA: Social Services (1990–2022), <https://doi.org/10.3886/ICPSR208207.V5>
NaNDA: Parks (2018, 2022), <https://doi.org/10.3886/ICPSR38586>

Both are released at the Census tract and the ZCTA level. We use the ZCTA files, because that is the closest thing to what the synthetic data can offer.
Which is the point to sit with: our file has ZIP codes, and NaNDA has ZCTAs. They look alike, five digits and usually the same five digits, and they are not the same thing. The next section is about that gap.

RStataPython



# How many rows carry a ZIP we can actually look something up with?
mydata %>%
  summarise(
    rows        = n(),
    has_zip     = sum(!is.na(zip)),
    missing_zip = sum(is.na(zip)),
    pct_missing = round(100 * mean(is.na(zip)), 1)
  )

# address, city and zip are each incomplete, and not for the same rows. A row
# with no ZIP may still have an address you could geocode, and the other way
# round, so "how much geography do I have" depends on which route you take.
(mydata
   .assign(address_missing=mydata["address"].isna(),
           city_missing=mydata["city"].isna(),
           zip_missing=mydata["zip"].isna())
   .value_counts(["address_missing", "city_missing", "zip_missing"])
   .rename("n")
   .reset_index()
   .sort_values("n", ascending=False))









NoteAside: what if you have addresses?



Street addresses are a different workflow, and we are not doing it today. You would geocode each address to coordinates, assign those coordinates to a Census tract, and use the tract-level NaNDA file, with failure modes of its own: addresses that will not parse, rooftop versus street-segment precision, and tract boundaries that also moved in 2020. The Census Bureau’s batch geocoder (https://geocoding.geo.census.gov/) is free, needs no API key, and returns the tract code directly, which skips the spatial join entirely. If your data have addresses, that tool plus Section 3 is most of what you need.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
The crosswalk we’re using

UDS Mapper ZIP Code to ZCTA Crosswalk (2019) — <https://web.archive.org/web/20220402144231/https://udsmapper.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/ZIPCodetoZCTACrosswalk2019.xlsx>
NaNDA’s own merge code: Chenoweth & Khan, code for merging NaNDA ZCTA-level datasets with the UDS Mapper crosswalk (2024), https://doi.org/10.3886/E124461V4

Use NaNDA’s published merge code rather than a snippet copied from a slide: it is citable, it is maintained, and when something needs fixing the fix lands in one place you can find again.

RStataPython



# Every column as text, for the same reason as `zip` above. Then pad back to five
# characters: whatever stripped a leading zero upstream did it before we got here.
zipzctaxwalk2019 <- read_excel(
  here("data", "zip_to_zcta_2019.xlsx"),
  col_types = "text"
) %>%
  mutate(
    ZIP_CODE = str_pad(ZIP_CODE, 5, pad = "0"),
    ZCTA     = str_pad(ZCTA,     5, pad = "0")
  )

# zip_join_type is the crosswalk telling you how each ZIP got its ZCTA — or that
# it has none. Read this before you join, not after something looks wrong.

mydata_zcta10 <- mydata %>%

import numpy as np
mydata_zcta10.assign(zcta_status=np.select(
    [mydata_zcta10["zip"].isna(), mydata_zcta10["zcta10"].isna()],
    ["no ZIP", "ZIP not in crosswalk"], default="has a ZCTA",
))["zcta_status"].value_counts()









ImportantWhich ZCTA vintage does your crosswalk target?



The 2019 release of the UDS Mapper ZIP Code to ZCTA Crosswalk targets 2010 ZCTAs. That makes it the right partner for the 2010-vintage NaNDA file and the wrong one for the 2020-vintage file. In the next section we join to both anyway, on purpose, because nothing in the code will tell you which of the two joins was mismatched. When you do this with your own data, read the crosswalk’s documentation for its target vintage before you read anything else.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
Carrying Social Services forward
Social Services ends in 2022; our data runs to 2025. Before joining, we give every ZCTA rows through 2025 and carry its most recent values into them. That is a decision, not a fix: the 2023 to 2025 rows will match, and what they match is 2022’s numbers. Write the decision down in your methods, because nothing in the output will.

RStataPython



# complete() adds the missing ZCTA-year rows; fill() carries each ZCTA's last
# value down into them. fill() does not stop at 2022: any value missing inside
# 1990-2022 (population, and the densities where population is zero) also gets
# the year before. Know that it happens.
socialservices_zcta10 <- socialservices_zcta10 %>%
  complete(zcta10, year = 1990:2025) %>%
  arrange(zcta10, year) %>%
  group_by(zcta10) %>%
  fill(everything(), .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup()

# Every year from 2022 on should now carry the same values.
tabyl(socialservices_zcta10, year) %>% filter(year >= 2020)

* Stata has no complete(); every ZCTA here has a 2022 row, so make three copies
* of it and number them 2023-2025. Then carry each ZCTA's last value down into
* anything still missing. Like R's fill(), that also reaches values missing
* inside 1990-2022 (population, and densities where population is zero).
use `socialservices', clear
expand 4 if year == 2022
bysort zcta10 year: replace year = 2021 + _n if year == 2022
sort zcta10 year
foreach v of varlist _all {
    if !inlist("`v'", "zcta10", "year") {
        by zcta10: replace `v' = `v'[_n-1] if missing(`v')
    }
}
save `socialservices', replace

* Every year from 2022 on should now carry the same values.

# pandas has no complete(); every ZCTA here has a 2022 row, so copy it to
# 2023-2025. Then carry each ZCTA's last value down into anything still missing.
# Like R's fill(), that also reaches values missing inside 1990-2022

ss_2022 = socialservices_zcta10[socialservices_zcta10["year"] == 2022]
socialservices_zcta10 = (
    pd.concat([socialservices_zcta10] + [ss_2022.assign(year=y) for y in (2023, 2024, 2025)])
    .sort_values(["zcta10", "year"])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
cols = socialservices_zcta10.columns.drop("zcta10")
socialservices_zcta10[cols] = socialservices_zcta10.groupby("zcta10")[cols].ffill()

# Every year from 2022 on should now carry the same values.
socialservices_zcta10.loc[socialservices_zcta10["year"] >= 2020, "year"].value_counts().sort_index()

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
The join

RStataPython



mydata_nanda <- mydata_zcta10 %>%
  # Social Services is longitudinal, so the key is ZCTA *and* year.
  # `in_nanda` is added before the join: it is TRUE on every row of the NaNDA
  # side, so after the join it is TRUE where something matched and NA where
  # nothing did. That is the diagnostic Stata hands you as `_merge` and dplyr
  # does not — if you want it, you build it.
  left_join(
    socialservices_zcta10 %>%
      select(zcta10, year, totpop, aland10,
             count_totindivfamilyservices, den_totindivfamilyservices,
             count_childyouthservices,     den_childyouthservices,
             count_elderservices,          den_elderservices) %>%
      mutate(in_nanda = TRUE),
    by = c("zcta10", "year")
  ) %>%
  mutate(in_nanda = coalesce(in_nanda, FALSE)) %>%
  # Parks is a single 2022 snapshot, so it joins on ZCTA alone and every year of
  # a person's records gets the same value. That is an assumption — that park
  # provision held still across the study period — not a free lunch.
  left_join(
    parks2022_zcta10 %>%
      select(ZCTA19, ANY_OPEN_PARK, COUNT_OPEN_PARKS_TC10, PROP_PARK_AREA_ZCTA),
    by = c("zcta10" = "ZCTA19")
  )

c(rows_before = nrow(mydata_zcta10), rows_after = nrow(mydata_nanda))

rows_before  rows_after 
       2004        2004

keep zcta10 year totpop aland10 ///
     count_totindivfamilyservices den_totindivfamilyservices ///
     count_childyouthservices     den_childyouthservices ///
     count_elderservices          den_elderservices
save `socialservices', replace

use `mydata_zcta10', clear
count
local rows_before = r(N)

* Social Services is longitudinal, so the key is ZCTA *and* year. Stata's
* _merge is the diagnostic the R version has to build by hand: 3 = matched,
* 1 = ours only. Keep it as in_nanda.
merge m:1 zcta10 year using `socialservices', keep(master match)
generate byte in_nanda = (_merge == 3)
drop _merge

* Parks is a single 2022 snapshot, so it joins on ZCTA alone and every year of
* a person's records gets the same value. That is an assumption, that park
* provision held still across the study period, not a free lunch.
preserve
    use `parks', clear
    keep ZCTA19 ANY_OPEN_PARK COUNT_OPEN_PARKS_TC10 PROP_PARK_AREA_ZCTA
    rename ZCTA19 zcta10
    save `parks', replace
restore
merge m:1 zcta10 using `parks', keep(master match) nogenerate

count
display "rows before = `rows_before', rows after = " r(N)
save `mydata_nanda'


# Social Services is longitudinal, so the key is ZCTA *and* year.
# merge(indicator=True) is the diagnostic Stata hands you as _merge: "both"
# where something matched, "left_only" where nothing did. Keep it as in_nanda.
mydata_nanda = (
    mydata_zcta10.merge(
        socialservices_zcta10[[
            "zcta10", "year", "totpop", "aland10",
            "count_totindivfamilyservices", "den_totindivfamilyservices",
            "count_childyouthservices",     "den_childyouthservices",
            "count_elderservices",          "den_elderservices",
        ]],
        how="left", on=["zcta10", "year"], indicator=True,
    )
    .assign(in_nanda=lambda d: d["_merge"].eq("both"))
    .drop(columns="_merge")
    # Parks is a single 2022 snapshot, so it joins on ZCTA alone and every year
    # of a person's records gets the same value. That is an assumption, that
    # park provision held still across the study period, not a free lunch.
    .merge(
        parks2022_zcta10[["ZCTA19", "ANY_OPEN_PARK", "COUNT_OPEN_PARKS_TC10", "PROP_PARK_AREA_ZCTA"]],
        how="left", left_on="zcta10", right_on="ZCTA19",
    )
    .drop(columns="ZCTA19")
)

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
section: Socioeconomic status: two files, split by year
text:
Socioeconomic status: two files, split by year
NaNDA’s SES measures are five-year ACS estimates, so each file’s value stands for a stretch of years. We split our rows at 2018. Rows through 2017 join the 2008–2017 file, published at 2010 ZCTAs. Rows from 2018 on join the 2018–2022 file, published at 2020 ZCTAs, and carry its values forward through 2025. Then the two halves are stacked back into one dataset.

RStataPython



# The two files name the affluence measure differently; give them one name
# before stacking.
mydata_nanda_le2017 <- mydata_nanda %>%
  filter(year <= 2017) %>%
  left_join(
    ses2008_2017_zcta10 %>%
      select(ZCTA10, AFFLUENCE13_17) %>%
      rename(AFFLUENCE = AFFLUENCE13_17),
    by = c("zcta10" = "ZCTA10")
  )

# Note: ZIP codes and ZCTAs can change geographically over time. These are
# 2010-vintage codes from the crosswalk, joined to a file drawn on 2020 ZCTAs.
mydata_nanda_ge2018 <- mydata_nanda %>%
  filter(year >= 2018) %>%
  left_join(
    ses2018_2022_zcta20 %>% select(ZCTA20, AFFLUENCE),
    by = c("zcta10" = "ZCTA20")
  )

mydata_nanda <- bind_rows(mydata_nanda_le2017, mydata_nanda_ge2018)

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
2010 vs 2020 ZCTAs, side by side
The note in that code is doing real work. The crosswalk gave us 2010 ZCTA codes, and from 2018 on we joined them to a file drawn on 2020 ZCTAs. To see what that costs, take the stack apart. What follows is not a demonstration of a mistake. It is the same join run twice, against the 2010-vintage NaNDA file and the 2020-vintage file, using the same crosswalked ZCTA codes, across every row. Both runs succeed. Both match the same rows, at the same rate, because most ZCTAs kept their five digits from one census to the next. What differs is the value each run attaches to those rows: the same people get a different mean affluence depending on which file was open. Nothing in either output identifies which run paired codes with the geography they were drawn for. That can only be answered from outside the code, by knowing what vintage each input carries.

    by = c("zcta10" = "ZCTA10")

    rows           = n(),
    matched        = sum(!is.na(AFFLUENCE)),
    match_rate_pct = round(100 * mean(!is.na(AFFLUENCE)), 1),
    mean_affluence = round(mean(AFFLUENCE, na.rm = TRUE), 3)

Read the table twice. The match rate is identical in both rows, so a match rate alone would never have told you anything was wrong. The mean moved. That is the shape of a vintage error: not a missing row you can count, but a plausible number attached to the wrong place.






WarningPick your vintage from your data, not from the file that happens to be open



The year your participants were observed decides the vintage, not the file that happens to be open. Observations through 2019 belong with 2010 geographies; from 2020 on, with 2020 geographies. Our synthetic file spans 2014–2025, so it straddles that boundary and also runs past the last year either NaNDA dataset covers. That is why the SES step above split the file by observation year and joined each part to its own file, and why Social Services was carried forward from its last available year with the decision written down. The one thing that split did not do is convert the codes: the 2018-on half still carries 2010 ZCTA codes into a 2020 file. For a real analysis you would run those rows through a 2020-target crosswalk first.

title: Linking NaNDA With Your Data
text:
Who did you lose?
A match rate is a headline, not a diagnostic. The headline above tells you the size of the loss and nothing about its shape. The diagnostic is whether the rows that did not match differ from the rows that did.
In this file about 17% of rows have no ZIP at all. If those rows are disproportionately rural, or older, or in worse health, the matched sample is no longer the sample you drew, and every neighborhood coefficient you estimate is conditional on having a mailable address. That is a selection problem, and it does not announce itself.
Neither language will do this for you. dplyr’s joins are silent. Stata’s _merge reports the count, not the composition. The comparison has to be made deliberately: isolate the unmatched rows, and put their means beside the matched rows’ means on the variables you actually care about.

# the reasons call for different answers: the first two are a data-collection
# problem, the third is a coverage limit you state in your methods, the fourth
# is usually a vintage mismatch. Three occur in this file; the third cannot,

unmatched %>%
  mutate(reason = case_when(
    is.na(zip)    ~ "no ZIP to start from",
    is.na(zcta10) ~ "ZIP not in the crosswalk",
    year > 2022   ~ "year past NaNDA's coverage",
    TRUE          ~ "ZCTA not in the NaNDA file"

# The rows that found no partner: the complement of the join, and the half
# nobody looks at. indicator="left_only" is the anti-join.
unmatched = (
    mydata_nanda.merge(
        socialservices_zcta10[["zcta10", "year"]].drop_duplicates(),
        how="left", on=["zcta10", "year"], indicator=True,
    )
    .query('_merge == "left_only"')
    .drop(columns="_merge")
)

# A count is not a diagnosis. A row can fail for four different reasons, and
# the reasons call for different answers: the first two are a data-collection
# problem, the third is a coverage limit you state in your methods, the fourth
# is usually a vintage mismatch. Three occur in this file; the third cannot,
# because we carried Social Services forward. It is named so the table says
# so if that step is ever dropped.
unmatched.assign(reason=np.select(
    [unmatched["zip"].isna(), unmatched["zcta10"].isna(), unmatched["year"] > 2022],
    ["no ZIP to start from", "ZIP not in the crosswalk", "year past NaNDA's coverage"],
    default="ZCTA not in the NaNDA file",
))["reason"].value_counts()



Three reasons appear, and they call for different responses. No ZIP is the big one and a data-collection problem; nothing downstream fixes it. The other two turn up twice each. A ZIP the crosswalk does not know is a typo or a ZIP newer than the crosswalk; a ZCTA the NaNDA file does not carry usually means the two were built on different vintages. At two rows apiece they vanish inside a match rate, and in real data they are the ones telling you something upstream is misaligned. That is why the table lists reasons, not just a count. The fourth reason, year past coverage, is absent only because we carried Social Services forward. Had we not, 407 rows would sit in that line, and the honest description of them is the same either way: a limit of the NaNDA file, handled by a decision you state in your methods.

section: A toy model, to show the join was for something
text:
A toy model, to show the join was for something
One model, not an analysis: does owning a pet go with the neighborhood measures we just attached? The service count is cut into bins so the coefficients read as comparisons against ZCTAs with none. Note the number of rows the model actually uses. Every unmatched row drops out here, silently, which is what the diagnostics above were for.

RStataPython



mydata_nanda <- mydata_nanda %>%
  mutate(count_totindivfamilyservices_6cat = cut(
    count_totindivfamilyservices,
    breaks = c(-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, Inf),
    labels = c("0", "1", "2", "3", "4-5", "6-10", "11+"),
    right = TRUE
  ))

own_pet_model <- glm(
  own_pet ~ hot_meal_days + count_totindivfamilyservices_6cat + ANY_OPEN_PARK + AFFLUENCE,
  data = mydata_nanda, family = binomial
)
summary(own_pet_model)
